research.summary: Free Adobe Acrobat Reader desktop Classic/perpetual release lines; excludes paid Adobe Acrobat (Pro/Standard), which is a separate product, and the subscription Continuous track
research.notes: Tier: researched (AGENTS.md rule 8b). Same reasoning as contributions/adobe-acrobat.json: no deterministic source covers this product (endoflife.date all.json has no acrobat or acrobat-reader slug as of 2026-09-17; no local record). Scope: the free Adobe Acrobat Reader desktop product only; paid Acrobat Pro/Standard is the separate product in contributions/adobe-acrobat.json, and its rows are deliberately absent here, so the two records never conflate the paid and free products even though both cite the same vendor matrix. Full-matrix inventory, not just the A-B section: the whole page was fetched (all A-B through S-Z sections) and every Reader-named row is published above. Reader 7.x, 8.x, 9.x, Reader X, Reader XI, Acrobat Reader 2015 (classic) and Acrobat Reader 2020 are the complete set of Reader rows on the matrix. Reader 2024 has no row anywhere on the page and no notice dates a Reader 2024 Classic, so no such line is asserted. Reader 2017 Classic is the one line the matrix omits while Adobe's own live notice still dates it verbatim (see that evidence quote); because it is an announced retirement with an explicit vendor date, it is published with its end of life 2022-06-06 and ga left null rather than dropped, per AGENTS.md rules 7 and 8b. Its date comes from the notice alone -- no matrix row exists to corroborate it -- which is exactly why the quote is stored beside it. No Reader release ever states an end of extended support: every Reader row carries N/A there, so eos and eossec stay null. Two matrix rows are excluded as different products: Reader Extensions Server (all platforms) 6.1 is a server product, not the desktop Reader, and the LiveCycle Reader Extensions ES/ES2/ES3/ES4 rows are LiveCycle server products. The subscription Continuous (evergreen Document Cloud) Reader track is excluded explicitly: it has no row on the vendor matrix, so it carries no published lifecycle date and none is invented. Where a cell carries an extension (2015: 4/7/2020 extended until 7/7/2020; 2020: 6/1/2025 extended until 11/30/2025) the extended date is stored as the end-of-life date, because it is the last date the vendor states the product is supported; the original core-support date is preserved verbatim in the quote beside it. Every matrix date is mm/dd/yyyy (the page's own note: All dates in mm/dd/yyyy format), so this contribution also needs the contribute.py day matcher to read US M/D/YYYY spellings. Adobe's own 2015 notice (/acrobat/kb/end-of-support-acrobat-2015-reader-2015.html, the page the matrix row itself links) now redirects to the Acrobat desktop hub and no longer states that date, so 2015 is cited to the matrix only.

research.summary: Paid Adobe Acrobat desktop (Pro and Standard) perpetual/Classic release lines; excludes the free Acrobat Reader and the subscription free-upgrade Continuous track
research.notes: Tier: researched (AGENTS.md rule 8b). endoflife.date has no acrobat product (checked https://endoflife.date/api/all.json 2026-09-17: no acrobat/acrobat-reader slug) and data/products/ holds no acrobat record; the existing data/products/coldfusion.json is a different Adobe product and is untouched. Scope: paid Acrobat desktop Pro/Standard lines only. Free Acrobat Reader is a separate product with its own contribution (contributions/adobe-acrobat-reader.json) and its Reader rows are deliberately absent here. The subscription Continuous (evergreen Document Cloud) track is excluded explicitly: it has no row on the vendor matrix at all (the matrix lists versioned lines only), so it carries no published lifecycle date and none is invented. Dates are the matrix's own cells: End of core support is the terminal supported date the vendor states, and where the cell carries an extension (2015, 2020: extended until 7/7/2020 and 11/30/2025) the extension is stored as the end-of-life date because it is the last date the product is supported, exactly as the matrix states it. End of extended support is N/A on every Acrobat row, so eos/eossec stay null. Every matrix Acrobat-named row is accounted for: 18 Pro/Standard/Pro Extended rows are published as 9 version cycles above; Acrobat & Review Comment Connector (1, 1.1) is a review connector, not a desktop Acrobat release; Acrobat 3D 8.x is an add-on that shipped with Acrobat 8; Acrobat Elements 7.x is an OEM/volume edition, not Pro or Standard; Acrobat Elements Server (6, 6.0.1) is a server product; Acrobat X Suite 10 is a bundle containing Acrobat X Pro and is not itself a Pro/Standard release (its 10 cycle dates are already published from the X Pro/X Standard rows). Every matrix date is mm/dd/yyyy (the page's own note: All dates in mm/dd/yyyy format); this contribution therefore also needs the contribute.py day matcher to read US M/D/YYYY spellings - requested from the engine owner with exact examples, see the handoff note. A date is never inferred: 2024's core support date is quoted as stated, and no other 2024 line is asserted. Adobe's own notice for Acrobat 2015 (/acrobat/kb/end-of-support-acrobat-2015-reader-2015.html, the link the matrix itself carries) now redirects to the Acrobat desktop hub and no longer states that date, so 2015 is cited to the matrix only; the X, XI, 2017 Classic and 2020 notice sentences above are quoted verbatim from the live notices Adobe still serves. Acrobat X Suite 10 and Acrobat Elements rows are excluded as bundles/OEM editions, and the Continuous (evergreen) track is excluded because the matrix carries no row for it.

research.summary: cPanel & WHM is a commercial Linux server automation and hosting management platform. The vendor documents current version lifecycle dates on a knowledge-base page; an optional deterministic TIERS.json feed provides LTS expiry timestamps, but only for LTS branches.
research.notes: The cPanel documentation page states "Approximate Release Date" and "Approximate End of Life Date" with month-precision values (e.g. 'March 2023', 'December 2026'). These are month-precision and stored as YYYY-MM without padding to a day, per AGENTS.md rule 4. The docs page only shows the four most recent release versions (110 LTS, 134 LTS, 136, 138); older versions' EOL dates are not on this page. A deterministic TSERS.json feed (https://httpupdate.cpanel.net/cpanelsync/TIERS.json) provides exact LTS expiry timestamps as Unix epoch values, but implementing a deterministic collector is a future enhancement; this contribution uses the docs page as the primary evidence source. Month-precision dates exclude these releases from the day-precision OpenEoX export, where they are enumerated under v1/openeox/index.json exclusions.

research.summary: ESET is a cybersecurity software vendor. The vendor publishes an End of Life policy page for business applications with two tables: 'Ongoing terminations' (applications scheduled for terminal EOL with End of Sale and End of Life dates) and 'Terminated applications' (applications already at EOL with End of Life dates). Coverage is sparse — many applications have 'Not available' or 'Not planned' dates. Day-precision dates are used where published.
research.notes: The ESET business EOL policy page lists applications in three categories: 'Applications at maintenance stage' (maintenance-only, not scheduled for EOL — excluded), 'Ongoing terminations' (scheduled for EOL with End of Sale and End of Life dates), and 'Terminated applications' (already at EOL with End of Life dates). Only applications with published day-precision dates are included. Many applications have 'Not available' or 'Not planned' dates and are excluded. The End of Sale date maps to eos and the End of Life date maps to eol (terminal support end). No GA dates are published for any application. Day-precision ISO dates are used directly. This contribution represents the subset of ESET business products with published EOL dates.

research.summary: The Kubernetes package manager. Each major branch is published separately: Helm 2 and Helm 3 carry the end dates their own project notices state, and Helm 4 carries none because the project has announced none.
research.notes: Full-picture coverage across the majors the Helm project has published lifecycle statements for. Helm 2: the deprecation timeline states no Helm v2 releases after November 13, 2020, even for security patches, so eossec and eol share that day; the project's own post of 2020-11-13 confirms the official end of support. Helm 3: the end-of-life notice states security fixes end February 10th, 2027 and that no releases of any kind follow, so eossec and eol share that day. Helm 4: undated. The release-schedule page announces release dates and the version-skew page states a rolling rule -- only the most recent minor release branch receives fixes -- and neither states an end date for any branch, so no Helm 4 date exists to publish and none was inferred. A rolling policy is compatibility guidance, not a lifecycle date, and is recorded here as the evidence for that absence rather than as a date. Helm 4.0.0 general availability (2025-11-12, per the project's GitHub release) is deliberately not published: the quoted notice does not state it, and every stored date must appear in a stored quote. No deterministic source covers Helm -- the upstream catalog publishes no Helm product and the official release calendar is machine-readable but carries release-planning events only, zero lifecycle events. ga and eos stay null on every branch because no quoted notice states them. Nothing here shadows a deterministic record.

research.summary: Caching/recursive DNS resolver by PowerDNS (PowerDNS.COM BV) — the Recursor product, separate from PowerDNS Authoritative Server, dnsdist and weakforced
research.notes: No deterministic source covers this product: endoflife.date lists 475 products and no Recursor/pdns slug, and the Recursor's own EOL page (doc.powerdns.com/recursor/appendices/EOL.html) is prose policy with <table count = 0 — it publishes no dated lifecycle table, which is the only reason no collector exists. This researched record exists because the vendor DOES publish dates elsewhere, at www.powerdns.com/support-commitment, whose Recursor grid has columns 'Release | First Customer Shipment (FCS) | Supported Commitment' and day-precision cells. Every date above is one of those cells quoted verbatim; nothing is derived. The EOL page itself points at that page ('Please refer to the support commitment for details on which versions are supported.'), which is why a source outside the product's own docs is admissible here. MODELING: one row per release TRAIN (5.5, 5.4, 5.3, 5.2, 5.1, 5.0, 4.x-and-older), matching engine/powerdns.py's train granularity for PowerDNS Authoritative Server, not one row per minor (the vendor grid lists 74 Recursor rows down to v5.4.6; a per-minor record would be ~74 lines of build metadata with no lifecycle meaning — trains are what the vendor's EOL statement and the one-year policy actually talk about). ga is the train's .0 FCS cell. eol is the vendor's own support end for the train: the terminal 'Support Commitment (until ...)' cell on the train's last listed minor, or the 'Discontinued Support (since ...)' cell on it once support has ended. NOT DERIVED: the relative policy quoted above ('critical updates for one year after the subsequent major release', and the 5.3/5.2 sentences) is stored as evidence and deliberately never converted into a date. It is corroboration only: the four train-end cells are exactly one year after the following train's .0 FCS (5.2.13's 2026-08-28 = 5.3.0 2025-08-28 + 1y; 5.1.10's 2026-01-14 = 5.2.0 2025-01-14 + 1y; 5.0.12's 2025-07-10 = 5.1.0 2024-07-10 + 1y; 5.3.10's 2027-03-09 = 5.4.0 2026-03-09 + 1y), but each stored date is the vendor's published cell, not our arithmetic. UNDATED ROWS: 5.4 is the current train and its last minor reads 'Support Commitment' with no end date, so eol stays null — an absent announcement is a fact, not a gap; 5.4's ga is dated from v5.4.0's FCS cell. 5.5 is a pre-release line (only 5.5.0-alpha1 exists); the notice covers it and ends it (pre-releases get no immediate security updates) but publishes no date, so it is published with no dates rather than dropped. 5.0's ga is null because the vendor's Recursor grid has NO v5.0.0 row (it starts at v5.0.1, 2024-01-10) and doc.powerdns.com/recursor/changelog/5.0.html has no 5.0.0 heading — only 5.0.0-rc1/rc2/beta1/alpha1 — so the train's GA day is unpublished and 5.0.1's FCS is not silently promoted into it. research.summary: Tyk Gateway is a Go-based open-source API gateway. The vendor publishes an explicit LTS release timeline with per-version support windows and end-of-life dates on its documentation site; there is no API or structured EOL feed.
research.notes: The vendor's LTS timeline table publishes month-precision support windows and EOL dates. The 'Completely Unsupported From' column states the EOL month (e.g. 'August 2026'); the end of the Maintenance Support Window (which still provides critical security fixes) marks eossec. GA dates are day-precision from the release notes page (e.g. '5 April 2024'). Month-precision eossec/eol dates are stored as YYYY-MM and never padded to day; they exclude these releases from the day-precision OpenEoX export, where they are enumerated under v1/openeox/index.json exclusions. Non-LTS minor versions reach EOL when the next minor is released (per the EOL policy); these are not enumerated here as the source gives no explicit per-version EOL dates for them.

research.notes: No deterministic source exists: endoflife.date has no Wasmtime product (475 products, no wasm identity), and the vendor's own lifecycle table at docs.wasmtime.dev/stability-release.html ships an empty static tbody -- every Version/Branch Date/Release Date/EOL Date row is produced in the browser by docs/js/index.js as 2024-04-20 plus (n-20) months, with +24 months for LTS and +2 months for normal releases. That is duration arithmetic, never a published date, so no collector is admissible. Dates here are the vendor's own explicit day-precision statements. Only releases the announcement itself dates are given dates: 24.0.0 (LTS, end of support 2026-08-20), 36.0.0 (LTS, 2025-08-20 to 2027-08-20), and 34.0.0, the one non-LTS line the notice ends explicitly (2025-08-20, at 36.0.0's release). 48.0.0 is the current LTS (released 2026-08-20) and carries no dates: the announcement predates it and publishes no deadline for it, so none is inferred. The remaining non-LTS branches (25-47) are governed only by the 2-month duration policy quoted below; that policy is stored as evidence and is never converted into a date, so those lines are not published with invented ends. ga for 24.0.0 and 48.0.0 stays null because no stored quote states it. Rendering defect: the live article page ends the 24.0.0 sentence at "until August 20," because the following "2026." was consumed as an ordered-list marker, so that one sentence is cited to the vendor's own published source file for the article rather than to the rendered page. Category framework follows the runtime precedent: endoflife.date categorizes the comparable runtimes nodejs, deno and bun as framework.
